claims.claim: Ex 1:1–5 repeats the list of Jacob's sons who came to Egypt and the total of seventy souls (cf. Gen 46:27).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:1–5, read in full

claims.claim: The LXX counts seventy-five souls at Ex 1:5 (NETS), reflecting the expanded list also in Gen 46:20 LXX and Acts 7:14.
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 1:5, read in full; Acts 7:14

claims.claim: The seventy (MT) vs seventy-five (LXX) difference comes from counting Joseph's descendants born in Egypt across his lifetime, including great-grandchildren (Machir, Gilead, Shuthelah, Ezer) who could not have existed at the entry.
claims.evidence: Augustine, CD XVI.40 (already in registry scope), read in full

claims.claim: Joseph, his brothers, and all that generation died before the oppression (Ex 1:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:6

claims.claim: Israel "were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; and the land was filled with them" (Ex 1:7) — the wording echoes the creation blessing (Gen 1:28) and the promise to Abraham (Gen 18:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:7; K&D Ex 1:7 (verbal parallels in the text)

claims.claim: "There arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph" (Ex 1:8) — the text names no king and gives no date.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:8

claims.claim: "New king" most naturally denotes a king ruling by different principles, not necessarily a new dynasty — though a dynasty change is the commonest explanation (Josephus Ant. 2.9.1; K&D).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 1:8 ("cannot be inferred with certainty... very probable"); Josephus Ant. 2.9.1

claims.claim: The king's fear was that in war Israel would join Egypt's enemies and leave the land (Ex 1:10) — emigration, not conquest, was his concern.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:10; K&D Ex 1:10

claims.claim: The taskmasters (*śārê missîm*) and the "treasure cities" (*miškĕnôt*) Pithom and Raamses (Ex 1:11) are the text's only named building works of the oppression.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:11; K&D Ex 1:11 (store-cities, not fortresses)

claims.claim: Pithom = Egyptian Pr-Itm ("House of Atum"); its site is disputed between Tell el-Maskhuta and Tell er-Retaba, with current opinion favouring Retaba for the Ramesside city.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries (Hoffmeier; Kitchen ch. 5) — NIV, background only

claims.claim: Raamses = Pi-Ramesses, the Delta capital of Ramesses II, at Qantir/Tell el-Dab'a (Bietak/Pusch) — a probable identification.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries (Hoffmeier; Kitchen ch. 5) — NIV, background only

claims.claim: The name "Raamses" was not in use before the 13th century BCE — the strongest single datum for a Ramesside setting (late-date argument); some argue the name reflects the time of writing.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries (Hoffmeier; Kitchen ch. 5) — NIV, background only

claims.claim: The LXX adds a third city, On (Heliopolis), to Ex 1:11 (NETS).
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 1:11, read in full

claims.claim: The oppression in "morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field" (Ex 1:14) matches Egyptian forced-labour practice attested in the Rekhmire tomb painting and Ramesside brick quotas.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries (Hoffmeier BAR 2012; Kitchen ch. 5) — NIV, background only; KJV Ex 1:14

claims.claim: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah (Ex 1:15) were Hebrew women, heads of the midwifery profession (K&D/JFB); Josephus's claim that they were Egyptian spies is rejected by Calvin and K&D.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:15 ("Hebrew midwives"); K&D Ex 1:15; JFB Ex 1:15; Calvin Ex 1:15–22; Josephus Ant. 2.9.2

claims.claim: The midwives "feared God" and saved the male children (Ex 1:17); God "made them houses" (Ex 1:21) — i.e., gave them families/posterity.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:17, 21; K&D Ex 1:21; JFB Ex 1:21; LXX "they made families for themselves" (NETS)

claims.claim: The midwives' answer to Pharaoh (Ex 1:19) was a falsehood; whether it was culpable is disputed — Augustine (*contra mendac.* 19, via K&D) says God rewarded their mercy, not their lie; Calvin agrees they lied and sinned; Lightfoot held it was no lie.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:19; K&D Ex 1:19 (Augustine quoted); Calvin Ex 1:15–22; Lightfoot via Calvin's editor's footnote — see §8.1

claims.claim: Pharaoh's final decree (Ex 1:22) commanded all his people to cast every Hebrew son into the river — an open, public order after the secret measures failed.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 1:22; Calvin Ex 1:15–22 (open violence after secret plots failed)

claims.claim: Amram (of Levi) married Jochebed (Ex 6:20; Num 26:59); Aaron and Miriam were born before the river decree.
claims.evidence: Ex 6:20; Num 26:59; K&D Ex 2:1–2; JFB Ex 2:1

claims.claim: Moses' mother hid him three months when she saw he was "a goodly child" (*tôb*; LXX *asteios*; Acts 7:20; Heb 11:23).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:2; NETS Ex 2:2; Acts 7:20; Heb 11:23

claims.claim: The basket was a *tēbâ* (H8392) of papyrus (*gōmeʾ*), daubed with bitumen (*ḥēmār*) and pitch (*zepet*) — the same noun as Noah's ark.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:3; BDB H8392 (28 occurrences, all Noah + Moses), read in full

claims.claim: The choice of *tēbâ* deliberately recalls Noah's ark (K&D; BDB notes the word occurs only in the two narratives).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 2:3; BDB H8392

claims.claim: Miriam watched from afar (Ex 2:4); JFB estimates she was ten to twelve years old.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:4; JFB Ex 2:4 (age estimate is JFB's, no textual basis)

claims.claim: Pharaoh's daughter came to bathe in the Nile; Egyptian royal bathing in the river is consistent with ancient Egyptian practice and the Nile's sanctity.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:5; K&D Ex 2:5; JFB Ex 2:5

claims.claim: Josephus names her Thermuthis (Ant. 2.9.6); rabbinic tradition calls her Bithiah; Jubilees calls her Tharmuth — the biblical text does not name her.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.9.6; Jubilees 47:3; K&D Ex 2:5 (Bithiah tradition)

claims.claim: The princess adopted Moses and named him Moses, "because I drew him out of the water" (Ex 2:10).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:10

claims.claim: The name Moses is Egyptian: Josephus (Ant. 2.9.6) derives it from Egyptian *mō* (= water) + *uses* (= saved); BDB notes Egyptian *mes/mesu* ("child, son") as the probable origin.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.9.6; BDB H4872, read in full; Philo Vit. Mos. I.17

claims.claim: Moses received a thorough Egyptian education ("in all the wisdom of the Egyptians," Acts 7:22); the tradition that he was a priest of Heliopolis named Osarsiph is unhistorical.
claims.evidence: Acts 7:22; K&D Ex 2:10 (Osarsiph rejected); Philo Vit. Mos. I.18–24 (royal education)

claims.claim: Josephus's Ethiopian campaign (Ant. 2.10) — Moses as general, the ibis stratagem, the siege of Saba, marriage to Tharbis — is an expansion with no basis in Exodus.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 2.10, read in full; K&D Ex 2:11 (unhistorical)

claims.claim: Moses, grown, killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew (Ex 2:11–12); he acted with deliberation ("looked this way and that way").
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:11–12

claims.claim: Moses' killing was a crime he had no legal authority to commit, yet it revealed a heart capable of virtue (Augustine, *c. Faustum* 22.70, via K&D); Philo calls it "a pious action" (Vit. Mos. I.44). The moral evaluation is disputed.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:12; K&D Ex 2:12 (Augustine quoted); Philo Vit. Mos. I.44 — see §8.2

claims.claim: The Hebrew's rebuke, "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" (Ex 2:14), shows the deed was known and Moses' authority rejected; Stephen cites it as Israel's rejection of their deliverer (Acts 7:25, 27–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:14; Acts 7:27–28

claims.claim: Moses fled to Midian in fear for his life (Ex 2:15); Heb 11:27 says he left Egypt by faith, "not fearing the wrath of the king" — K&D reconciles: the faith was in renouncing Egypt, not in the manner of flight.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:15; Heb 11:27; K&D Ex 2:15 (reconciliation)

claims.claim: Midianites descend from Abraham through Keturah (Gen 25:2, 4); Jethro's branch lived in the southern Sinai peninsula, within reach of Horeb.
claims.evidence: Gen 25:2, 4; K&D Ex 2:15 (geography)

claims.claim: The priest of Midian is called Reuel in Ex 2:18 and Jethro in Ex 3:1; the commonest resolution is that Reuel is the proper name and Jethro a title/surname (K&D); Clarke conjectured Reuel was dead and Jethro his successor (brother-in-law).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:18, 3:1; K&D Ex 2:18; Clarke Ex 3:1 — see §8.10

claims.claim: Reuel ("friend of God") served the old Semitic God El (K&D); Jethro is plausibly a Kenite (cf. Judg 1:16; 4:11; JVL Kenite article).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 2:18; Judg 4:11; JVL Kenite (registry-verified, read in full)

claims.claim: Moses married Zipporah and named his first son Gershom, "I have been a stranger in a strange land" (Ex 2:21–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:21–22

claims.claim: A second son, Eliezer ("God is my help"), is named only in Ex 18:4, not in Ex 2; the Vulgate interpolates his birth here.
"In process of time, the king of Egypt died" (Ex 2:23) — whether this king is the "new king" of Ex 1:8 or a successor cannot be decided from the text.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:23; K&D Ex 2:23

claims.claim: "God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob... and God had respect unto them" (Ex 2:24–25).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 2:24–25

claims.claim: Moses kept Jethro's flock and "came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb" (Ex 3:1); Horeb is the mountain group of southern Sinai, "mount of God" by anticipation of the later theophany.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:1; K&D Ex 3:1; JFB Ex 3:1

claims.claim: The "angel of the LORD" appeared "in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush" (Ex 3:2); the text then identifies the speaker as Jehovah (3:4) — the Angel is Jehovah himself, not a created angel.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:2, 4; K&D Ex 3:2; Clarke Ex 3:2

claims.claim: The bush (*sĕneh* H5572) was a thorny bush, perhaps a blackberry/bramble (BDB); it burned and was not consumed (Ex 3:2–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:2–3; BDB H5572, read in full

claims.claim: The burning bush symbolises Israel in the fire of affliction, not consumed because God is in its midst.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 3:2; JFB Ex 3:2; Clarke Ex 3:2; Philo Vit. Mos. I.65–70 — see §8.4

claims.claim: "Put off thy shoes... the place whereon thou standest is holy ground" (Ex 3:5) — removal of sandals as reverence/confession of unworthiness; the custom is widely attested in the ancient East.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:5; K&D Ex 3:5; JFB Ex 3:5; Clarke Ex 3:5

claims.claim: "I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Ex 3:6) — the singular "thy father" gathers the three patriarchs as one; Stephen quotes it in the plural (Acts 7:32).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:6; K&D Ex 3:6; Clarke Ex 3:6; Acts 7:32

claims.claim: Moses hid his face, "for he was afraid to look upon God" (Ex 3:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:6

claims.claim: God had "seen the affliction," "heard their cry," and "come down to deliver them" to "a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey" (Ex 3:7–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:7–8

claims.claim: The six nations listed in Ex 3:8 (Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites) match the Gen 10:15 / Gen 15:20–21 lists; the Girgashites are absent here.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:8; K&D Ex 3:8

claims.claim: Moses' first objection, "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" (Ex 3:11), was answered by "Certainly I will be with thee" and the sign that Israel would serve God on this mountain (Ex 3:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:11–12

claims.claim: The promised sign (serve God on this mountain, Ex 3:12) is forward-looking: its fulfilment lies in the Sinai covenant (Ex 19; 24), not in the burning bush itself.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:12; K&D Ex 3:12; Clarke Ex 3:12

claims.claim: Moses' second question, "What is his name?" (Ex 3:13), presupposes that a name discloses nature and deed, not mere curiosity about a label.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:13; K&D Ex 3:13; Calvin Ex 3:10–17

claims.claim: "I AM THAT I AM" (*ʾehyeh ʾăšer ʾehyeh*; H1961) — God as self-existent and eternal, "I will be what I will be" (Calvin: future tense with the force of the present, designating perpetual duration; K&D: "the absolute God... acting with unfettered liberty").
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:14; BDB H1961, read in full; K&D Ex 3:14; Calvin Ex 3:10–17 — see §8.5

claims.claim: The LXX renders Ex 3:14 "Egō eimi ho Ōn" — "I am The One Who Is" (NETS).
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 3:14, read in full

claims.claim: "This is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations" (Ex 3:15) — the name in view is YHWH, the God of the fathers (Calvin: it cannot refer to "I am that I am" itself; K&D agrees the name explained is YHWH).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:15; K&D Ex 3:15; Calvin Ex 3:10–17

claims.claim: Ex 6:3 ("by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them") stands in tension with the patriarchal use of YHWH in Genesis; the standard resolution is that the patriarchs knew the name but not its full redemptive meaning.
The elders of Israel were the heads of families/tribes, the nation's representatives; they formed a court of magistrates from Joseph's time (Clarke).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:16; K&D Ex 3:16; Clarke Ex 3:16

claims.claim: "I have surely visited you" (Ex 3:16) fulfils Joseph's dying words, "God will surely visit you" (Gen 50:24) — the same Hebrew idiom.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:16; Gen 50:24; K&D Ex 3:16; Clarke Ex 3:16

claims.claim: The request for a three days' journey to sacrifice (Ex 3:18) was a genuine first step, not a deception: God knew Pharaoh's heart and revealed his purpose in stages (K&D/Hengstenberg, citing Augustine, *Quaest.* 13 in Ex.).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:18; K&D Ex 3:18 — see §8.6

claims.claim: "I am sure that the king of Egypt will not let you go, no, not by a mighty hand" (Ex 3:19 KJV) — the Hebrew *wĕlōʾ* is better read "except/unless by a mighty hand" (Vulgate *nisi*; LXX *ean mē*; NETS; Clarke; Calvin's Latin *nisi in manu forti*).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:19; NETS Ex 3:19; K&D Ex 3:19; Clarke Ex 3:19; Calvin Ex 3:10–17

claims.claim: The "spoiling of the Egyptians" (Ex 3:21–22): *šāʾal* means "ask, demand," not "borrow" (K&D/Clarke/Calvin); *hišʾîl* means "to grant a request," not "to lend" (K&D/Knobel).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 3:21–22; NETS Ex 3:22; K&D Ex 3:22; Clarke Ex 3:22; Calvin Ex 3:10–17

claims.claim: The spoiling was recompense for unpaid labour, not theft: the Israelites had built Pithom and Raamses without compensation (Clarke).
claims.evidence: Clarke Ex 3:22; K&D Ex 3:22 (gift of divine favour) — see §8.7

claims.claim: The three signs (rod→serpent, leprous hand, water→blood) were given to convince Israel, strengthen Moses' faith, and later confront Pharaoh.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:1–9; K&D Ex 4:1–9

claims.claim: The rod became a serpent, which Moses fled, then seized by the tail, and it became a rod again (Ex 4:2–5).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:2–5

claims.claim: The second sign — the hand leprous as snow, then restored — signifies Israel's afflicted, defiled state and God's power to purify it (K&D, after Kurtz/Theodoret).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 4:6–7

claims.claim: The third sign — Nile water poured on dry land becoming blood — struck at the Nile, honoured by Egyptians as divine.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:9; K&D Ex 4:9 (Hengstenberg on Osiris)

claims.claim: "A voice is ascribed to the sign" (Ex 4:8) — the signs speak as witnesses to Moses' commission.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:8; K&D Ex 4:8

claims.claim: Moses' plea, "I am not eloquent... slow of speech, and of a slow tongue" (Ex 4:10), denotes a defect of utterance or difficulty in fluent Egyptian after long disuse (JFB); not exactly "stammering" (K&D).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:10; JFB Ex 4:10; K&D Ex 4:10 — see §8.11

claims.claim: God's answer, "Who hath made man's mouth? ... I will be with thy mouth" (Ex 4:11–12), asserts divine sovereignty over human faculties.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:11–12

claims.claim: Moses' final plea, "send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send" (Ex 4:13), was a refusal of the mission; "the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses" (Ex 4:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:13–14

claims.claim: JFB's reading that the anger was shown by transferring the priesthood from Moses to Aaron is a distinctive inference, not stated in the text.
claims.evidence: JFB Ex 4:14; K&D Ex 4:14 (does not draw it)

claims.claim: Aaron "can speak well" and was already coming to meet Moses (Ex 4:14); "thou shalt be to him instead of God" (Ex 4:16) — Moses as the inspiring God to Aaron as prophet.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:14–16; K&D Ex 4:16; cf. Ex 7:1

claims.claim: Moses returned to Jethro and asked leave without disclosing the divine commission (Ex 4:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:18; K&D Ex 4:18; JFB Ex 4:18

claims.claim: "All the men are dead which sought thy life" (Ex 4:19) — the death of the Pharaoh of Ex 2:15 removed the proscription.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:19; JFB Ex 4:19 (the "429th year" is JFB's chronology — Traditional)

claims.claim: Moses set out with his wife and sons (Ex 4:20) — the plural "sons" confirms a second son already born, though his birth is not narrated until Ex 18:4.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:20; K&D Ex 4:20

claims.claim: "I will harden his heart" (Ex 4:21) — the hardening is ascribed to God ten times and to Pharaoh himself ten times in Exodus; Pharaoh's own hardening precedes God's (first five plagues), and divine hardening begins at the sixth (Ex 9:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:21; K&D Ex 4:21 — see §8.8

claims.claim: "Israel is my son, even my firstborn" (Ex 4:22) — sonship by election/adoption, not physical generation; the title implies the calling of the nations (first-born among sons).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:22; K&D Ex 4:22

claims.claim: The lodging-place attack (Ex 4:24–26) — "the LORD met him, and sought to kill him" — is the most obscure passage in the category; the cause (the uncircumcised son) is inferred from Zipporah's act, not stated.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:24–26; K&D Ex 4:24; Calvin Ex 4:24–31 — see §8.9

claims.claim: The LXX of Ex 4:24 reads "an angel of the Lord met him" (NETS), against MT "the LORD met him."
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 4:24, read in full

claims.claim: Zipporah circumcised her son with a stone (*ṣûr*) and cast the foreskin at Moses' feet, saying "a bloody husband art thou to me" (Ex 4:25) — addressed to Moses, not the son (K&D/Calvin); the LXX renders the phrase as "the blood of the circumcision of my child is staunched" (NETS).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:25; NETS Ex 4:25; K&D Ex 4:25; Calvin Ex 4:24–31 — see §8.9

claims.claim: Moses had neglected the circumcision to please his Midianite wife (K&D/Calvin); the neglected son was the younger, probably Eliezer (Calvin; K&D says the elder was already circumcised).
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 4:24; Calvin Ex 4:24–31 — see §8.9

claims.claim: Moses then sent his wife and sons back to Jethro, inferred from Ex 18:2 (K&D/JFB); the text of Ex 4 does not state it.
claims.evidence: Ex 18:2; K&D Ex 4:26; JFB Ex 4:26

claims.claim: Aaron met Moses "in the mount of God" (Ex 4:27) after a separation of forty years (JFB); they kissed, and Moses told Aaron all God's words and signs (Ex 4:28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:27–28; JFB Ex 4:27 ("forty years" from Acts 7:23, 30)

claims.claim: Aaron spoke to the elders and did the signs; "the people believed... and bowed their heads and worshipped" (Ex 4:30–31) — but this faith did not stand the test of Ex 5.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 4:30–31; K&D Ex 4:31

claims.claim: The LXX of Ex 4:31 adds that the people "were glad" (NETS) — the reading behind Knobel's proposed emendation of MT *yišmĕʿû* to *yiśməḥû* (K&D).
claims.evidence: NETS Ex 4:31, read in full; K&D Ex 4:31

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) names "Israel" as a people in Canaan — the earliest extra-biblical mention of Israel — setting a terminus ante quem for any Exodus; it does not date the Exodus itself and does not mention Moses.
claims.evidence: Secondary summaries (Hoffmeier; Kitchen ch. 5) — NIV, background only; see §6.3 and §7.1

connections.note: The seventy souls; the bridge from Genesis.
The multiplication and the affliction foretold to Abram; "come out with great substance."
The death of Joseph's generation closes the patriarchal age; the new king follows.
The land of Raamses (Goshen) as the place of settlement and of the building.
Civil disobedience out of fear of God — the midwives and the three friends.
*Tēbâ* — the ark of bulrushes and Noah's ark; the same noun, the same deliverance through water.
Egyptian naming and adoption — Moses and Joseph, both given Egyptian names at court.
Stephen's retelling of the killing, the rebuke, and the flight.
Midian, son of Keturah; the Midianites' Abrahamic descent.
The well scene — Moses and Jacob, both meeting their future wives at a well.
"God remembered his covenant" — the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
"God will surely visit you" — Joseph's dying words fulfilled in the remembering.
Horeb, the mountain of God — the mountain of the call is the mountain of the covenant.
"I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father" — the same formula to Jacob at Bethel.
"I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" — Jesus' argument for the resurrection.
"Ye shall serve God upon this mountain" — the sign fulfilled at Sinai.
"Before Abraham was, I am" — the *Egō eimi* of the divine name.
"I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur" — YHWH revealed at the covenant (K&D's link).
"I will smite Egypt with all my wonders" — foretold, then fulfilled in the plagues.
The spoiling foretold, then fulfilled at the departure.
The rod-serpent before Israel (by Moses) vs before Pharaoh (by Aaron) — Stackert notes the source tension; the connection is recorded with the note, not suppressed.
"Thou shalt be to him instead of God" (4:16) → "I have made thee a god to Pharaoh... Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet" (7:1–2).
The threat to Pharaoh's first-born, fulfilled at the Passover.
"Israel is my son" → "when Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" (also Matt 2:15, in the notes).
The circumcision covenant — the sign whose neglect brings the attack.
The people's belief, immediately tested by the increased oppression.
The faith chapter — Moses' parents, Moses' refusal of Pharaoh's daughter, the reproach of Christ.
"Him that dwelt in the bush" — Moses' blessing recalls the theophany.
The waters of death reversed — the river decree and the Red Sea.
The name — "I did not make known" — the tension carried forward.
The infant massacre and the flight — Herod's slaughter and the flight into Egypt, a reversal of Moses' flight out.
The divine name proclaimed at the bush, proclaimed again at Sinai ("The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious").

title: Israel's Oppression and Moses' Early Life
